tierWindow.goal: Put the critical skills to work: analyse an interpretation into its parts, evaluate its relative value against alternatives, and synthesise several sources into an argument of your own.
tierWindow.cognitiveDemand: Application and analysis (apply, analyse, evaluate, synthesise) on well-framed academic sources.
tierWindow.taskComplexity: Several parts held together at once; applying a named skill to a source rather than only recognising it.
tierWindow.autonomy: Moderate scaffolding; worked examples that model the skill, then guided application the learner performs; feedback explains the reasoning.

decidedValue.priorExperienceAnchor: The learner has met the critical mindset at the introductory tier: they can explain what being critical is, tell active engagement from passive, and use the basic language of criticality (analysis, evaluation, synthesis, judgement). This course assumes that vocabulary and turns it into skills the learner performs on sources.

subThemes.label: Reading academic sources critically: engaging with the structure of a journal article rather than taking its conclusion whole
Analysis in action: breaking an interpretation, body of evidence or data set into its parts through close examination
Evaluation in action: weighing the relative value of one factor or interpretation against alternatives
Synthesis in action: drawing different interpretations and evidence together in forming and expressing your own argument
Telling the three skills apart: what each move asks and how they build on one another
Discipline-specific vocabulary: the words that carry meaning within a subject's own critical discourse

decidedValue.signpostBody: The course has three short lessons, one for each skill. First, analysis: taking a source apart to see its claim, evidence and reasoning. Second, evaluation: weighing an interpretation against alternatives. Third, synthesis: drawing several sources into an argument of your own. Work through them in order; each skill builds on the one before.
decidedValue.signpostInstruction: Work through the three lessons in order.
decidedValue.overview:
This course is about the critical skills in action. You already know what being critical means and that it is a mindset. Here you put three of its core moves to work: analysis, evaluation and synthesis.

These are the skills university assignments ask for by name. Being able to perform them, not just recognise them, is what moves your work from reporting what sources say to building a case of your own.
decidedValue.courseOutcomesFraming: Three course outcomes framed up front: analyse a source, evaluate an interpretation, synthesise several sources.

practiceConnection.academic: Analysis, evaluation and synthesis are the engine of academic work. Every essay that asks you to evaluate a theory, every literature review that draws sources together, every seminar where interpretations are weighed, runs on these three skills. Build them now and they carry into every module of your degree, and into the reasoned judgement that professional work later asks of you.

grounding.note: W-OPEN states the three course outcomes and why they matter (AL-5)

decidedValue.whereNextBody: One direction goes deeper and others go wider. Going deeper: the advanced criticality course takes these skills into articulating criticality in your own voice, across whole pieces of writing. Going wider: analysis, evaluation and synthesis underpin Academic Writing, Researching and Research Methods, and Reflective Practice, where you put them to work on real tasks.
decidedValue.summary: You have reached the end of the course. The critical skills are no longer just words: they are moves you can make. You can analyse a source by separating its claim, evidence and reasoning; evaluate an interpretation by weighing its relative value against alternatives, with reasons; and synthesise several sources into an argument of your own. Look back at the confidence check: comparing where you started with where you are now shows how far this has moved.

practiceConnection.academic: From here, analysis, evaluation and synthesis are what you practise in every module. Each time a brief says analyse or evaluate, each literature review that draws sources together, each argument you build rather than report, is these skills at work. They are also what research and professional practice reward: the ability to take evidence apart, weigh it, and build a reasoned case travels well beyond your degree.

courseReferences.title: See pages 117 to 133 of Chapter 8, 'Critical thought and developing a critical edge in writing', of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).

items.stem: To analyse an academic source means mainly to...
A student separates an article's central claim from the evidence behind it and the reasoning that links them. Which critical skill is this?
A student judges that one interpretation accounts for the evidence better than a rival, and gives reasons. Which critical skill is this?
A student sets two sources that agree against a third that dissents, and builds a claim none of them stated alone. Which critical skill is this?
